reason: The sources provide sufficient details to support a 45-second script with more than 10 verified claims.
story: In 1963, astronomers were baffled by an enigmatic, star-like object cataloged as 3C 273. Its spectrum defied classification, showing bizarre, unidentifiable lines. Then astronomer Maarten Schmidt realized the truth: those lines were normal hydrogen, but stretched massively by a staggering redshift. 3C 273 was flying away from Earth at a fraction of the speed of light, placing it an astonishing 2.4 billion light-years away. To be visible from that unimaginable distance, this point of light had to be trillions of times brighter than the Sun. Scientists soon discovered it was the first identified quasar, powered by a colossal supermassive black hole consuming material at its galactic core, shooting out a 200,000-light-year jet, and hiding in plain sight in the constellation Virgo for amateur telescopes to spot.
angle: A faint point of light visible through amateur backyard telescopes is actually a monstrous quasar 2.4 billion light-years away, outshining the Sun by trillions of times.

claims.claim: 3C 273 was the first quasar ever to be identified.
It is located approximately 2.4 to 2.5 billion light-years away from Earth.
Maarten Schmidt published the breakthrough paper reporting its substantial redshift in 1963.
It is visually the brightest quasar in the Earth's sky.
It has an apparent visual magnitude of approximately 12.9.
It is bright enough to be observed through a 6-inch amateur telescope.
The quasar is over 4 trillion times more luminous than the Sun at visible wavelengths.
It features a large-scale visible jet measuring roughly 200,000 light-years long.
Quasars are powered by supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies.
The name 3C 273 signifies the 273rd object of the Third Cambridge Catalog of Radio Sources.
Its central supermassive black hole is estimated to have a mass of roughly 885 to 900 million solar masses.
It lies at the center of a giant elliptical host galaxy in the constellation Virgo.

disputed: The exact mass of the central supermassive black hole varies slightly depending on measurement techniques, ranging between approximately 885 million to 900 million solar masses (or wider historical estimates), and should be stated with appropriate approximations.
